title: Glean Alternative With On-Premise Deployment and Audit Logs
summary: Glean's cloud-only architecture, missing query-level audit logs, and probabilistic RAG make it indefensible in SOC and regulatory audits. Here's what regulated buyers need instead.
body_markdown:
### Summary


- Glean fails regulated buyers on three structural grounds: cloud-only deployment with no true air-gapped option, admin-level audit logs with no query-level record, and probabilistic cosine-similarity retrieval that can return a different answer to the same question.
- Glean licensing runs roughly $45–65 per user per month with typical multi-year minimums, while Jinba Flow's deterministic workflows run at $5–20 per month at scale versus $300+ for a stochastic AI agent equivalent.
- Five criteria decide whether an AI tool creates audit risk or removes it: data residency, query-level audit logging, answer consistency, self-managed deployment, and versioned workflow integration.
- Before your next regulatory review, test whether you can reconstruct exactly what your AI presented to a decision-maker.[Jinba](https://jinba.io/) deploys on-premise in air-gapped environments and logs every query, retrieved record, and response.


For banks, insurers, and legal teams, every new AI tool is a new audit surface. The question procurement and compliance teams ask is whether every decision the tool supports can be defended when a regulator asks.


Glean fails that test on three structural grounds. Its architecture is cloud-only, with no true on-premise or air-gapped deployment. Its audit logs cover administrator activity rather than the query-level record of who asked what, which documents were returned, and what the AI said in response. Its retrieval method,[cosine-similarity RAG](https://www.glean.com/cosine-similarity) , is probabilistic, which means the same question can return different answers on different days. In a regulated workflow, that is an indefensible process.


## What Glean's Deployment Models Actually Permit


[Glean's own documentation](https://docs.glean.com/get-started/prepare/about-deployment) describes exactly two deployment options: "Glean Hosted," a standard SaaS instance on Google Cloud, and "Customer Hosted," which places Glean's tenant inside the customer's own AWS or GCP VPC. The second option is not traditional self-hosting. Glean retains responsibility for infrastructure management and support access. Customers cannot manually patch, modify, or air-gap the architecture. For any bank or insurer whose data residency policy prohibits sensitive client records from leaving its own controlled environment, both options are disqualifying.


Glean does ship an[admin audit log](https://docs.glean.com/administration/management/audit-logs/admin-audit-logs) accessible from the Admin Console. It records administrator actions: permission changes, connector configurations, user management events. It does not record the sequence a regulator needs: which user submitted a query, which documents the system retrieved, and what answer was generated. That record does not exist in Glean at the query level.


The pricing compounds the risk. Third-party analysis places Glean's licensing at[roughly $45–65 per user per month](https://onyx.app/insights/glean-alternatives) , typically with multi-year minimums. A tool that cannot be air-gapped, cannot provide a query-level audit trail, and carries escalating renewal commitments is a defensibility problem rather than a cost one.


## Three Regulated Workflows Where the Architecture Matters


### A Compliance Officer Running KYC Queries


A compliance officer at a large bank is investigating whether a high-net-worth client has undisclosed connections to Politically Exposed Persons. The investigation draws on internal client notes, transaction records, and screening reports. Every step must be logged and reproducible. The bank's data policy prohibits sensitive client information from leaving its on-premise environment.


Glean's cloud-only models eliminate it from consideration before the first query is run. Even setting residency aside, the audit problem is decisive. When a regulator asks for the exact information presented to the officer when the client was cleared, Glean cannot produce it. There is no query-level log. The bank cannot reconstruct the decision-making basis. If a second reviewer runs the same query the following day, the cosine-similarity retrieval can surface different document chunks and generate a materially different summary. The verification process breaks down.


[Jinba](https://jinba.io/) deploys on-premise inside the bank's air-gapped data center. No data leaves the controlled environment.[Jinba App](https://app.jinba.io/) and[Jinba Flow](https://flow.jinba.io/) generate a full, SOC II compliant audit log for every workflow execution: user identity, timestamp, query text, and the specific validated records returned.[Jinba Brain](https://jinba.io/brain) is not RAG. It stores company knowledge as ontology-validated records built on the FIBO Financial Industry Business Ontology standard. The same query returns the same verified facts every time, regardless of when or by whom it is run.


### An Insurance Underwriter Pulling Policy Context


An underwriter is reviewing a large commercial property damage claim. The question is whether a specific category of water damage is excluded under the active policy, which carries several endorsements. An incorrect determination could expose the insurer to a multi-million dollar liability.


The underwriter queries Glean for the relevant exclusion clause. The system's cosine-similarity retrieval finds two closely worded clauses: one from the active policy and one from a superseded template stored in the same document corpus. It synthesises an answer that draws from both. The underwriter proceeds on that basis. If the decision is later challenged in litigation, the insurer cannot prove what the AI presented, cannot show which version of the policy was consulted, and cannot demonstrate that the answer was derived from a verified source. The decision is not auditable and therefore not defensible.


Jinba Brain stores policy information using the ACORD Information Model for insurance. A query for an exclusion clause retrieves the precise structured record tied to that policy number and version. There is no ambiguity introduced by semantic similarity across documents. Each record carries its source path and a SHA-256 hash of the originating document, providing an unbroken chain of evidence from raw data to final answer. The underwriting check itself runs as a deterministic workflow in Jinba Flow: 80% rule-based, consistent across every execution, and costing $5–20 per month at scale rather than $300 or more for a stochastic AI agent equivalent.


### A Legal Team Reviewing Contracts at Scale


A corporate legal team must review 10,000 vendor contracts to identify every instance of a "limitation of liability" clause that deviates from the firm's standard template. The task is rule-based: a clause either meets the template criteria or it does not, regardless of how it is worded.


Cosine-similarity retrieval is designed for semantic proximity rather than legal rule enforcement. It will flag clauses that use similar vocabulary but carry different legal meaning, and it will miss clauses that are structurally non-compliant but worded unusually. The margin for error in a review of this scale is not acceptable.


The configuration problem compounds this. The legal team refines its search criteria in Glean's admin panel over several months. When a later audit reveals that a specific subset of contracts was missed, the team attempts to trace the configuration state at the time of the review. The change was not captured in Glean's audit log. The failure cannot be diagnosed, reconstructed, or defended.


[Jinba Flow's](https://flow.jinba.io/) visual editor lets the legal team encode the exact logic for identifying non-compliant clauses as a deterministic workflow. That workflow is published as a reusable service. Every change to the workflow is version-controlled with a full revision history. An auditor can retrieve the exact version of the logic applied to any specific contract at any point in the review. Non-technical paralegals invoke the approved workflow through[Jinba App's](https://app.jinba.io/) chat interface, with access governed by role-based permissions. The platform separates building from execution, so the validated logic runs consistently regardless of who triggers it.

## What the Next Audit Will Actually Ask


The three scenarios above share a common structure. A regulated professional makes a consequential decision supported by an AI tool. A regulator or auditor later asks: "Show us exactly what the system presented, and prove it was derived from a verified, authorised source."


Glean cannot answer that question. Its cloud-only architecture means the data may not have been permitted to reach the system in the first place. Its admin-level audit logs do not capture the query sequence. Its probabilistic retrieval means the answer the system gave cannot be reproduced on demand.


For regulated enterprises evaluating a Glean alternative, the selection criteria are concrete. The tool must deploy on-premise or in a fully controlled private environment. It must log every query, every retrieved record, and every generated response in a tamper-evident trail. It must produce the same answer to the same question regardless of when it is run or who runs it. It must also encode business logic as versioned, auditable workflows rather than prompts that re-infer the rules on every execution.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Why is Glean not suitable for banks, insurers, and legal teams?


Glean creates audit risk on three structural grounds: it is cloud-only with no true air-gapped option, its audit logs cover administrator activity rather than query-level records, and its cosine-similarity retrieval is probabilistic. Together, these mean a regulated team cannot guarantee that sensitive data stayed inside the perimeter, cannot reconstruct what the AI presented to a decision-maker, and cannot reproduce the same answer on demand. For workflows that must be defensible to a regulator, each of these is disqualifying on its own, and Glean fails all three.


### Does Glean offer an on-premise or air-gapped deployment?


No. Glean offers only two deployment models: "Glean Hosted" on Google Cloud and "Customer Hosted," which places Glean's tenant inside the customer's own AWS or GCP VPC. "Customer Hosted" is not true self-hosting: Glean retains operational control and support access, and customers cannot air-gap or manually patch the architecture. Any organisation whose data residency policy prohibits sensitive records from leaving its controlled environment will find both options non-compliant.


### What is the difference between a query-level audit log and Glean's admin audit log?


An admin audit log records administrator actions such as permission changes and connector configurations. A query-level audit log records what happened during a workflow: which user submitted a query, which documents were retrieved, and what answer the system generated. Glean provides the former but not the latter. When a regulator asks exactly what information was presented to an officer who cleared a client, Glean cannot produce the record, because it does not exist.


### Why is probabilistic retrieval a problem in a regulated workflow?


Because the same question can return different answers on different days, making the decision path impossible to reproduce. Cosine-similarity RAG retrieves document chunks based on semantic proximity, so a second reviewer running an identical query can surface different passages and generate a materially different summary. In a KYC check, an underwriting decision, or a contract review, that destroys the ability to verify, diagnose, or defend the original decision.


### What should regulated buyers look for in a Glean alternative?


Regulated buyers should evaluate five criteria: (1) data residency (true on-premise or air-gapped deployment); (2) audit logging (a tamper-evident, query-level trail of every query, retrieved record, and AI response); (3) answer consistency (deterministic outputs that are identical regardless of when or by whom they are run); (4) deployment model (self-managed and auditable rather than a closed managed service); and (5) workflow integration (versioned, auditable business logic instead of prompts that re-infer rules on every run).


### How does Jinba guarantee the same query returns the same answer?


Jinba Brain does not use cosine-similarity RAG. It stores company knowledge as ontology-validated records built on established standards: the FIBO Financial Industry Business Ontology for banking and the ACORD Information Model for insurance. A query retrieves the precise structured record tied to the relevant entity, policy, or template, so there is no ambiguity introduced by semantic similarity across documents. The same query returns the same verified facts every time, and each record carries its source path and a SHA-256 hash for an unbroken chain of evidence.


### How much does Glean cost compared to Jinba?


Third-party analysis places Glean's licensing at roughly $45–65 per user per month, typically with multi-year minimums. Jinba Flow's deterministic workflows run at $5–20 per month at scale, compared with $300 or more for a stochastic AI agent equivalent. The larger point for regulated buyers is that Glean's cost escalates on multi-year commitments for a tool that still cannot be air-gapped or provide a query-level audit trail: a defensibility problem rather than a pricing one.


### Is Jinba SOC II compliant and can it run on-premise?


Yes. Jinba is SOC II compliant and deploys on-premise, including inside air-gapped data centres, so no data leaves the controlled environment. Jinba App and Jinba Flow generate a full SOC II compliant audit log for every workflow execution, capturing user identity, timestamp, query text, and the specific validated records returned. This lets an auditor reconstruct any decision from the log alone.


### Can Jinba handle KYC, underwriting, and contract review workflows?


Yes, these are exactly the regulated workflows Jinba is built for. Compliance officers can run KYC queries with full reproducibility, underwriters can retrieve the precise exclusion clause tied to a policy's number and version, and legal teams can encode contract-review rules as versioned deterministic workflows invoked through role-based access. In each case, the validated logic runs consistently regardless of who triggers it, and every execution is logged and auditable.
